nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

questions.q: An auditor asks who is responsible for hypervisor patching, physical-data-centre security, customer's EC2 guest OS hardening, and customer's IAM-policy design. The customer answers with one model published by AWS. Which is the correct division?
choices: AWS manages every layer of the stack — hardware, hypervisor, network, guest OS, customer applications
Customers run physical datacentre security and operate the AWS global backbone network
AWS secures the cloud; customers secure what they put IN the cloud
AWS handles every compliance and regulatory requirement transparently for the customer
questions.explanation: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (hardware, facilities, global infrastructure). Customers are responsible for security IN the cloud (data, IAM, OS patching on EC2, etc.). The other options are incorrect: AWS manages every layer of the stack — hardware, hypervisor, network, guest OS, customer applications, IAM, and data — leaving customers no operational duties. Customers run physical datacentre security and operate the AWS global backbone network, while AWS only provisions virtual machines from the customer-built fleet. AWS handles every compliance and regulatory requirement transparently for the customer, with no shared duties on data, identity, or operating-system configuration.

questions.q: A startup wants the LOWEST latency for users in Tokyo, São Paulo, and Frankfurt. The architect proposes deploying the same application stack in AWS Regions geographically close to each user population (e.g., ap-northeast-1, sa-east-1, eu-central-1). What is the PRIMARY benefit of using these distinct Regions?
choices: Lower latency to nearby users PLUS regional data-residency
Automatic synchronous replication of all services across every Region
Identical published prices across every Region
Free inter-Region data transfer for all active-active workloads
questions.explanation: Deploying into geographically closer Regions reduces latency for nearby users and supports data-residency requirements. AWS does NOT automatically replicate services across Regions; each service requires explicit configuration (S3 CRR, DynamoDB Global Tables, etc.). Per-Region pricing varies. Inter-Region traffic is billable. The other options are incorrect: Automatic synchronous replication of all services across every Region — false; cross-Region replication is optional, not the primary benefit of multi-Region deployments for user latency. Identical published prices across every Region — false; per-Region pricing varies and lower latency for local users is the primary benefit of geographic distribution. Free inter-Region data transfer for all active-active workloads — false; inter-Region transfer incurs data-transfer charges and is not a default benefit for users.

questions.q: AWS infrastructure inside one Region is partitioned into multiple physically isolated facility groups, each with its OWN power, cooling, and network — connected to each other by sub-ms private fibre. A Region typically has 3+ of these. What's the AWS term for one of these facility groups?
choices: Availability Zone — one or more discrete data-centre facilities with independent power
Region — the geographic area that contains and groups the AZs
Edge Location / CloudFront POP — a global edge-cache facility outside the Region structure
VPC subnet — a customer-defined logical network segment inside an AZ
questions.explanation: An AZ is one or more data centers within a Region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Multiple AZs in a Region enable high availability architecture. The other options are incorrect: Region — the geographic area that contains and groups the AZs; Regions share no power, cooling, or networking across their constituent AZs. Edge Location / CloudFront POP — a global edge-cache facility outside the Region structure; not an independently power- and cooling-isolated data-centre grouping. VPC subnet — a customer-defined logical network segment inside an AZ; not a physical power- and cooling-independent facility; subnets group connected IP address ranges sharing the AZ's underlying infrastructure.

questions.q: A cloud-101 lecture defines a property as: 'resources can be ADDED or REMOVED automatically in response to demand signals, and you pay only for actual usage'. This contrasts with the on-prem paradigm of static, over-provisioned peak capacity. Which cloud property is this?
choices: Manual capacity stretching of on-prem hardware bought ahead of demand — not a cloud property
Automatic scaling up AND down with demand, paying for actual usage — the textbook elasticity property
Annual long-horizon capacity planning with a fixed reserved allocation — a traditional procurement model
Static fixed allocation reserved for peak load even when actual demand is low — the opposite
questions.explanation: Elasticity = dynamically scale resources with demand + pay for actual usage. The other options are incorrect: Manual capacity stretching of on-prem hardware bought ahead of demand — not a cloud property; this is the traditional fixed-allocation model that does not scale with actual usage. Annual long-horizon capacity planning with a fixed reserved allocation — a traditional procurement model; it does not automatically scale with actual usage or represent a cloud elasticity property. Static fixed allocation reserved for peak load even when actual demand is low — the opposite of the cloud elasticity property; resources are provisioned regardless of actual usage.

questions.q: An auditor asks AWS who is responsible for: (1) the physical security of the data centre, (2) hypervisor patching, (3) the customer's EC2 guest OS patching, (4) the customer's application data encryption. Which mapping is correct under the Shared Responsibility Model?
choices: Customer owns ALL four items
AWS owns ALL four items
Mapping varies by support tier
AWS = security OF the cloud; Customer = security IN the cloud
questions.explanation: AWS: physical security, data center facilities, networking hardware, hypervisor, and managed service infrastructure. Customer: everything they put in the cloud — data encryption, IAM, OS patching on EC2, network config. The other options are incorrect: Customer owns ALL four items — incorrect; AWS owns the security of the cloud foundation including datacentre, hardware, hypervisor, and network. AWS owns ALL four items — incorrect; customers own security IN the cloud, including guest OS patching, IAM, data, and application configuration. Mapping varies by support tier — incorrect; the shared-responsibility model is fixed and not influenced by which support tier the account holds.

questions.q: An architect designing for high availability must distinguish two AWS scope concepts: (1) a geographic area containing multiple isolated data-centre clusters connected by low-latency fibre, (2) one or more of those data-centre clusters in distinct power/cooling/network failure domains. Which mapping is correct?
choices: Both Region and AZ are interchangeable labels for the same physical datacentre
A Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones
A Region is a load-balancer pool and an AZ is the IP subnet managed by that pool
A Region is a marketing label with no physical separation between its AZs
questions.explanation: A Region (e.g., us-east-1) is a geographic cluster of AZs. An AZ (e.g., us-east-1a) is one or more data centers with independent infrastructure. Multi-AZ deployments protect against single data center failure. The other options are incorrect: Both Region and AZ are interchangeable labels for the same physical datacentre — false; a Region is a geographic area grouping multiple Availability Zones each with independent power and cooling infrastructure. A Region is a load-balancer pool and an AZ is the IP subnet managed by that pool — false; a Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated AZs, not a load-balancing construct. A Region is a marketing label with no physical separation between its AZs — false; a Region is a real geographic area whose multiple AZs are physically isolated facilities.

questions.q: Under the Shared Responsibility Model, for a Lambda function deployed in customer code, who is responsible for: (a) hypervisor patching, (b) Lambda runtime (e.g., python3.12) patching, (c) the customer's function CODE, (d) the IAM role attached, (e) the data the function reads/writes?
choices: Customer owns the Lambda runtime and underlying OS
Customer handles only OS patching for Lambda
Lambda is identical to EC2 in the Shared Responsibility Model
AWS handles infrastructure, OS, and runtime patching
questions.explanation: Serverless shifts more responsibility to AWS. For Lambda, you don't manage: servers, OS, runtime patches, capacity. You still own: your code, IAM roles, data encryption, network access, and application-level security. The other options are incorrect: Customer owns the Lambda runtime and underlying OS — false; AWS manages and patches the Lambda runtime, operating system, and underlying compute; the customer owns the function code, IAM role, and data. Customer handles only OS patching for Lambda — false; AWS handles OS patching; the customer is responsible for the function code, the IAM role permissions, and the data processed by the function. Lambda is identical to EC2 in the Shared Responsibility Model — false; Lambda is more managed than EC2; on EC2 customers own OS patching and runtime; on Lambda those responsibilities shift to AWS, leaving the customer responsible for function code, IAM role, and data.

questions.q: A workload in a single AZ is taken offline when that AZ has a utility-power incident. The architect spreads the workload across 3 AZs in the same Region. Why does this design eliminate the single-AZ failure?
choices: AZs are labels for the same datacentre with no real physical isolation or single-failure boundary
AZs share power, cooling, and network feeds
AZs are physically separate facilities with independent power, cooling, and network
Multi-AZ deployments always double the cost regardless of architecture
questions.explanation: Each AZ is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power/network. They're connected with low-latency links but isolated from each other's failures. Multi-AZ = high availability. ELB + Auto Scaling + RDS Multi-AZ = HA architecture. The other options are incorrect: AZs are labels for the same datacentre with no real physical isolation or single-failure boundary — false; AZs are physically separate facilities with independent failure domains so a single AZ failure does not cascade. AZs share power, cooling, and network feeds — false; each AZ has independent power, cooling, and connectivity so that a single utility failure in one AZ does not affect the others. Multi-AZ deployments always double the cost regardless of architecture — false; cost depends on the specific service and configuration; deploying across AZs is the standard architecture for high availability without necessarily doubling overall cost.

nodes.title: Host a static website on AWS

data.scenario: You have a folder of static HTML/CSS/JS. Serve it worldwide over HTTPS on your own domain, with no servers to manage.

nodes.explanation: Store the files in S3, serve them globally over HTTPS through CloudFront, then point your custom domain at the distribution with Route 53.

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

flashcards.front: Why use server-side encryption?
flashcards.back: Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

flashcards.front: What's storage durability vs availability?
flashcards.back: Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

questions.q: A team needs durable OBJECT storage for any size of file, REST-API-accessible, with 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability and globally addressable URLs. They don't need a POSIX filesystem. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon EBS — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance
Amazon S3 — object storage with 11-nines durability, HTTPS REST access
Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS filesystem shared across EC2 instances
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host
questions.explanation: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's object storage service. It stores data as objects in buckets, offers 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EBS — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance; not globally addressable via URLs or designed for 11-nines durability. Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS filesystem shared across EC2 instances; not globally addressable via REST URLs with 11-nines object durability. EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host; data is lost on stop or termination and is not globally addressable.

questions.q: A team has medical imaging files that are accessed about 4× per year but, when accessed, must be retrievable in MILLISECONDS (not hours). They want to pay less than S3 Standard storage rates. Which S3 storage class fits?
choices: S3 Standard-IA — same millisecond retrieval as Standard at a lower per-GB storage rate with a per-GB
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval — minutes-to-hours retrieval times
S3 Standard — millisecond retrieval and lowest retrieval cost but the most expensive per-GB storage tier
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — hours-long retrieval and the cheapest storage
questions.explanation: S3 Standard-IA is for data accessed less frequently but needs immediate access when required. Lower storage cost than S3 Standard but retrieval fee applies. The other options are incorrect: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval — minutes-to-hours retrieval times; cheaper storage but does not meet the millisecond-retrieval requirement for the medical imaging files. S3 Standard — millisecond retrieval and lowest retrieval cost but the most expensive per-GB storage tier; ill-suited for the infrequent-access pattern described. S3 Glacier Deep Archive — hours-long retrieval and the cheapest storage; not a millisecond-retrieval tier for the medical imaging files described.

questions.q: A relational database on EC2 needs PERSISTENT block storage that survives instance stop/start AND can be reattached to a different instance in the same AZ. The storage must be a /dev/sdX block device the OS formats with a filesystem. Which AWS storage primitive fits?
choices: Amazon S3 — durable object storage with an HTTPS REST API
Amazon EBS — persistent block storage volume that outlives
Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS file system shared across instances
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host
questions.explanation: EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage volumes attached to EC2. Unlike instance store, EBS persists after instance stop/terminate and can be detached/reattached. The other options are incorrect: Amazon S3 — durable object storage with an HTTPS REST API; not persistent block storage and not attachable to EC2 as a block device that survives instance stop. Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS file system shared across instances; not a persistent single-instance block volume that presents as a raw block device. EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host; data is lost on stop or termination and cannot be detached and reattached to another instance the way EBS volumes can.

questions.q: A fleet of 12 EC2 web servers in 3 AZs must SHARE one writable filesystem so user uploads written by one server are immediately visible to the others. The filesystem must be POSIX with NFS-mount semantics, scale storage automatically, and be regional (multi-AZ). Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon EFS — elastic NFS file system that mounts across many EC2 instances
Amazon EBS — single-instance persistent block storage
Amazon S3 — durable object storage
AWS Storage Gateway tape archive — a virtual tape library for backup workflows
questions.explanation: EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed NFS file system that can be mounted to multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones simultaneously. Unlike EBS which attaches to one instance. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EBS — single-instance persistent block storage; multi-attach is limited to a few instances in the same AZ and is not designed as a writable shared filesystem across many instances in multiple AZs. Amazon S3 — durable object storage; accessible from any EC2 instance via REST API but not a POSIX writable filesystem mountable across a fleet. AWS Storage Gateway tape archive — a virtual tape library for backup workflows; not a writable shared filesystem for active production use across a fleet of web servers.

questions.q: A bucket holding critical compliance docs is at risk of accidental overwrite/delete by the application or by an admin. The team wants to retain a HISTORY of every object version, recover prior versions, and undelete tombstoned objects. Which S3 feature?
choices: Bucket-creation order counter — not a real S3 feature
Bucket-policy history — would track IAM-policy change versions if it existed
S3 Versioning — retains every version of every object; PUT and DELETE create new versions
S3 Object-level CloudTrail — audits API call events against objects including deletes but does not
questions.explanation: S3 Versioning stores all versions of an object including writes and deletes. Enables recovery from accidental overwrites/deletes. Can be used with Lifecycle policies to manage costs. The other options are incorrect: Bucket-creation order counter — not a real S3 feature; S3 does not keep an ordered creation counter or versions of bucket-creation events. Bucket-policy history — would track IAM-policy change versions if it existed; S3 does not natively retain versions of policy documents or deletion events. S3 Object-level CloudTrail — audits API call events against objects including deletes but does not retain previous version content or enable restoration of an earlier object version.

questions.q: A compliance archive of CT scan images must be retained 30 years. Access frequency is well below 1 read per year. Retrieval latency may be 12 hours. Minimum storage cost is the only optimisation criterion. Which S3 storage class fits?
choices: S3 Glacier Deep Archive — lowest per-GB cost, multi-hour retrieval, ideal for 30-yr cold archive
S3 Standard — the most expensive per-GB storage class with millisecond retrieval
S3 Intelligent-Tiering — auto-tiers objects based on access patterns but adds a per-object monitoring cost
S3 One Zone-IA — single-AZ infrequent-access storage at a lower cost than Standard
questions.explanation: S3 storage classes by access frequency: Standard > Intelligent-Tiering > Standard-IA > One Zone-IA > Glacier Instant > Glacier Flexible Retrieval > Glacier Deep Archive. Match access pattern to class to minimize costs. The other options are incorrect: S3 Standard — the most expensive per-GB storage class with millisecond retrieval; not appropriate for a 30-year archive with infrequent access where cost efficiency is the primary driver. S3 Intelligent-Tiering — auto-tiers objects based on access patterns but adds a per-object monitoring cost; the access pattern here is known and rare enough that Deep Archive's lower cost wins. S3 One Zone-IA — single-AZ infrequent-access storage at a lower cost than Standard; it has a higher per-GB cost than Deep Archive and lacks multi-AZ redundancy for a 30-year retention requirement.

questions.q: A team needs MANAGED file systems for specific protocols: SMB for Windows file shares, Lustre for high-performance computing, NetApp ONTAP for migration from on-prem ONTAP, OpenZFS for ZFS workloads. They want one AWS service family that covers all four. Which?
choices: A new EBS volume type — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance
Amazon FSx — managed file-system family that covers each of those
Amazon EFS — managed NFS (NFSv4) file system only
AWS Storage Gateway — exposes S3 as an on-prem file and tape gateway
questions.explanation: FSx is the managed file-systems family: Windows File Server (SMB), Lustre (HPC), NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS. Storage Gateway is different (hybrid). The other options are incorrect: A new EBS volume type — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance; it does not cover managed protocol-specific file systems for SMB, Lustre, or NetApp ONTAP workloads. Amazon EFS — managed NFS (NFSv4) file system only; it does not cover the SMB, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, or OpenZFS protocols offered by the FSx managed file-system family. AWS Storage Gateway — exposes S3 as an on-prem file and tape gateway; it covers only on-prem bridge scenarios and does not provide cloud-native Windows SMB shares, Lustre HPC, or ONTAP managed by FSx.

nodes.title: Compute services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

flashcards.front: What is autoscaling?
flashcards.back: A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.

flashcards.front: Reserved / committed-use vs on-demand pricing.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

questions.q: A developer needs to run a Python function in response to S3 object-creation events with NO server to provision, NO OS to patch, billing in 1 ms increments only when the function runs. Which AWS service fits?
choices: AWS Lambda — serverless function-as-a-service: event-driven, no infra, per-ms billing
Amazon EC2 — a virtual-machine service that bills for provisioned capacity
Amazon ECS — a container-orchestration service that still requires provisioning a cluster
Amazon Lightsail — a bundled small-VM service with a flat monthly billing model
questions.explanation: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service. You upload code and Lambda runs it in response to events. You pay only for execution time — no server management required. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EC2 — a virtual-machine service that bills for provisioned capacity regardless of whether the function is executing; the customer manages the infra. Amazon ECS — a container-orchestration service that still requires provisioning a cluster; per-function event-driven billing is not part of its model. Amazon Lightsail — a bundled small-VM service with a flat monthly billing model; it is not an event-driven function-as-a-service.

questions.q: A web tier sized for steady traffic gets bursty afternoon spikes. The team wants the fleet to GROW to absorb peak and SHRINK when demand drops, automatically based on CPU and request-count metrics, without operator intervention. Which AWS feature?
choices: EC2 instance-family swap — a manual right-sizing step performed on each instance
Automated OS patching via Systems Manager — applies security patches automatically but does not
AWS Auto Scaling — automatically adds or removes instances based on demand signals such as CPU
Scheduled RDS / EBS snapshots — automated backup operations that run on a time-based schedule
questions.explanation: AWS Auto Scaling monitors applications and automatically adjusts capacity (EC2 instances, ECS tasks, etc.) to maintain performance and minimize costs. The other options are incorrect: EC2 instance-family swap — a manual right-sizing step performed on each instance; it does not automatically add or remove capacity in response to traffic spikes. Automated OS patching via Systems Manager — applies security patches automatically but does not automatically scale capacity up or down based on load. Scheduled RDS / EBS snapshots — automated backup operations that run on a time-based schedule; they protect data but do not respond to request volume or automatically add compute capacity on demand.

questions.q: A web tier has 6 EC2 instances serving HTTPS. A new release introduces autoscaling — at peak the fleet may grow to 30, at trough shrink to 3. The team needs a managed service that automatically registers/deregisters scaling instances and distributes inbound HTTPS requests with health checks. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon CloudFront — a CDN that distributes cached content to edge locations
Amazon RDS read-replica — distributes read queries across database replicas
Amazon Route 53 weighted records — DNS-level distribution of queries
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes inbound to EC2 / containers / IP
questions.explanation: ELB distributes traffic across multiple targets. ALB (Application) = Layer 7/HTTP, NLB (Network) = Layer 4/TCP, GLB (Gateway) = Layer 3 for third-party appliances. Integrates with Auto Scaling. The other options are incorrect: Amazon CloudFront — a CDN that distributes cached content to edge locations; it is not a back-end load balancer that distributes inbound HTTPS requests to EC2 instances with health checks. Amazon RDS read-replica — distributes read queries across database replicas; it is not a component that distributes inbound HTTPS traffic to web-tier EC2 instances. Amazon Route 53 weighted records — DNS-level distribution of queries; it does not perform per-request inbound traffic distribution or health-check-based instance selection.

questions.q: A small dev team wants to deploy a Node.js web app to AWS without configuring the underlying EC2 / LB / autoscaling / health-checks themselves. They upload the source, AWS provisions everything based on the platform, scales it, and updates it. Which AWS service fits?
choices: Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane
Amazon ECR — managed container image registry
AWS CDK — Infrastructure-as-Code tool that synthesises CloudFormation
AWS Elastic Beanstalk — PaaS that provisions EC2, load balancer
questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS that deploys web apps (Java, .NET, PHP, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go, Docker). You upload code; Beanstalk handles the infrastructure. You still control the underlying resources. The other options are incorrect: Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane; the team still configures autoscaling policies, health checks, and deploy pipelines manually rather than getting them provisioned automatically. Amazon ECR — managed container image registry; it stores and versions container images but does not provision load balancers, Auto Scaling, or platform updates. AWS CDK — Infrastructure-as-Code tool that synthesises CloudFormation; the team still provisions and manages the underlying infrastructure and platform updates.

questions.q: A backend must orchestrate this flow: (1) start a Lambda, (2) wait for human approval, (3) run a Glue ETL job, (4) on success notify SNS, (5) on failure invoke a different Lambda. The flow is long-running, has retries with exponential backoff, and is auditable. Which service?
choices: AWS Lambda chained directly with synchronous invocations only — possible but lacks built-in state
Amazon SQS alone — provides reliable queueing primitives but no built-in orchestration, branching
AWS Step Functions — managed state-machine workflow orchestrator with built-in retries, branching
Amazon EventBridge alone — event bus that routes events between services but offers no built-in retries
questions.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates distributed applications as state machines with visual workflows. Coordinates Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SNS, SQS, and more with built-in error handling and retries. The other options are incorrect: AWS Lambda chained directly with synchronous invocations only — possible but lacks built-in state tracking, automatic retries, and visual workflow representation for the steps. Amazon SQS alone — provides reliable queueing primitives but no built-in orchestration, branching, or visual representation of multi-step workflow logic. Amazon EventBridge alone — event bus that routes events between services but offers no built-in retries, branching, or visual orchestration of a multi-step workflow.

questions.q: A pre-baked OS image with a specific Linux distro, kernel version, pre-installed nginx + Python venv, and security-hardened config is published as a reusable EC2 image. Launching a new EC2 from this image gives you that EXACT environment. What is this template called?
choices: AWS Management Console — browser-based admin UI for AWS
An Amazon Machine Image — template that EC2 uses to provision new instances
An asymmetric key-pair — used to SSH into a Linux instance after launch
A VPC template — defines a virtual network (CIDR, subnets, route tables)
questions.explanation: An AMI is the EC2 launch template: it bundles a root volume snapshot, launch permissions, and a block-device mapping. AMI ≠ the browser management console. The other options are incorrect: AWS Management Console — browser-based admin UI for AWS; not the pre-baked OS image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software. An asymmetric key-pair — used to SSH into a Linux instance after launch; not the OS-image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software. A VPC template — defines a virtual network (CIDR, subnets, route tables); not the OS-image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software.

questions.q: A first Lambda invocation after a long idle period shows 800 ms of added latency. The next invocation a second later finishes in 30 ms. The 800-ms first-hit overhead is documented as the time to provision a new execution environment, download the deployment package, start the runtime, and run any module-level init. Which Lambda phenomenon is this?
choices: Region cold start — a hypothetical one-time environment provisioning event that would affect all
Billing first-invocation surcharge — not a real Lambda billing item
Cold start — execution-environment provisioning, runtime load
Execution timeout — a hard limit that terminates a too-long invocation at the END of its runtime
questions.explanation: Lambda cold start = time to provision container + load runtime + init your code. Mitigation: Provisioned Concurrency (keeps environments warm), Lambda SnapStart (Java), smaller deployment packages, faster runtimes (Node/Python vs Java). The other options are incorrect: Region cold start — a hypothetical one-time environment provisioning event that would affect all invocations across the Region simultaneously after a long idle period; not an invocation-specific init latency spike. Billing first-invocation surcharge — not a real Lambda billing item; Lambda bills per request and duration; the startup latency is a cold start init event, not a billing surcharge. Execution timeout — a hard limit that terminates a too-long invocation at the END of its runtime; not the added init and runtime provisioning latency at the start of a cold invocation.

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

flashcards.front: What is a landing zone?
flashcards.back: A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: An ops team wants automated recommendations across COST (idle resources, RI coverage), PERFORMANCE (under-provisioned instances), SECURITY (open SGs, root MFA), FAULT TOLERANCE (no Multi-AZ), and SERVICE LIMITS (approaching quotas) — refreshed continuously and surfaced in the console. Which AWS service?
choices: External pen-test firm — a manual security engagement
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses resource-based policies for unintended external access
AWS Organizations — multi-account governance with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing
AWS Trusted Advisor — automated checks across five pillars with actionable recommendations
questions.explanation: Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and provides actionable recommendations. Basic checks (free): S3 bucket permissions, MFA on root account. Full checks require Business or Enterprise support. The other options are incorrect: External pen-test firm — a manual security engagement; it does not provide automated checks across cost optimisation, fault tolerance limits, or performance efficiency pillars. AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses resource-based policies for unintended external access; it does not emit cost, performance, or fault-tolerance recommendations across multiple service-pillar checks. AWS Organizations — multi-account governance with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing; it does not perform automated checks across the cost, fault tolerance, performance, and limits pillars.

questions.q: A compliance team needs the AWS service that: (a) takes a snapshot of every resource's CONFIGURATION over time, (b) evaluates each snapshot against rules (e.g., 'S3 bucket must have versioning enabled'), (c) surfaces drift with timeline + non-compliant flag. Which service?
choices: AWS Systems Manager — manages running EC2 instances via patching, session manager, and run command
AWS Config — records resource configuration history and evaluates against rules
AWS CodeDeploy — deploys application code to EC2 or Lambda targets
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses IAM grants for unintended external access
questions.explanation: AWS Config is the configuration-recording / rule-evaluation service. CodeDeploy deploys application code. Systems Manager is run-time admin. The other options are incorrect: AWS Systems Manager — manages running EC2 instances via patching, session manager, and run command; it does not record resource configuration history or evaluates account-wide compliance rules against snapshots. AWS CodeDeploy — deploys application code to EC2 or Lambda targets; it does not track resource configuration history or evaluate AWS resources against compliance rules. AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses IAM grants for unintended external access; it does not record general resource configuration history or evaluate resources against custom compliance rules.

questions.q: A company has 40+ AWS accounts. They want one place to: (a) create new accounts, (b) cluster them into OUs, (c) apply guardrails via Service Control Policies, (d) consolidate billing into one invoice. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS IAM Identity Center — workforce SSO and permission-set assignment across multiple AWS accounts
AWS Migration Hub — tracks application migrations across AWS tools
AWS Organizations — central multi-account management plane with OUs, Service Control Policies
AWS Auto Scaling — coordinates dynamic capacity scaling across multiple AWS services
questions.explanation: AWS Organizations enables centralized management of multiple AWS accounts: consolidated billing (volume discounts), Service Control Policies to restrict account permissions, and account grouping in OUs. The other options are incorrect: AWS IAM Identity Center — workforce SSO and permission-set assignment across multiple AWS accounts; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, SCPs, and billing. AWS Migration Hub — tracks application migrations across AWS tools; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, Service Control Policies, and consolidated billing. AWS Auto Scaling — coordinates dynamic capacity scaling across multiple AWS services; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing.

questions.q: Inside AWS Organizations, a permission GUARDRAIL applies at the OU or account level. It can DENY (or filter) what any IAM principal — including the account's root user — is allowed to do. It does NOT grant permissions, only caps them. Which construct is this?
choices: An IAM identity-based policy attached to users, groups, or roles
A Service Control Policy (SCP) at the OU or account scope — the GUARDRAIL that caps maximum permissions
A VPC-level network ACL filtering subnet traffic — an account-level networking control
A CloudFormation template that provisions account resources — IaC for deploying infrastructure
questions.explanation: SCPs are the AWS Organizations guardrail: they cap (deny / filter) the maximum permissions for IAM principals in the targeted OU / account, including the account's root user. They never GRANT — they only restrict. The other options are incorrect: An IAM identity-based policy attached to users, groups, or roles — grants permissions within a single account; it does not cap the maximum permissions across an OU or multiple accounts like an SCP. A VPC-level network ACL filtering subnet traffic — an account-level networking control; it does not cap IAM permissions or enforce account-level permission guardrails. A CloudFormation template that provisions account resources — IaC for deploying infrastructure; it does not enforce permission caps or serve as a permission guardrail across accounts.

questions.q: An architect new to AWS asks where to find AWS's prescriptive best-practice guidance, organised into pillars that an architecture review can score against (with detailed lenses for serverless, machine-learning, SaaS, IoT). Which official AWS resource is this?
choices: AWS Marketplace — catalogue of third-party software and SaaS listings for purchase
AWS Well-Architected Framework — six pillars plus domain-specific lenses with prescriptive
AWS Service Catalog — lets internal admins curate approved CloudFormation templates for end users
AWS Solutions Library — pre-built reference implementations for common workloads
questions.explanation: The Well-Architected Framework helps architects build secure, high-performing, resilient, and efficient infrastructure. Use the Well-Architected Tool in the AWS console for free architectural reviews. The other options are incorrect: AWS Marketplace — catalogue of third-party software and SaaS listings for purchase; it does not host AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars or framework guidance. AWS Service Catalog — lets internal admins curate approved CloudFormation templates for end users; it does not host AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars or framework guidance. AWS Solutions Library — pre-built reference implementations for common workloads; useful examples, but not the canonical place for AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars and lenses.

questions.q: A company has Oracle, SQL Server, and Windows Server licences they own (BYOL). They want a managed inventory tool that tracks each license, attaches them to AWS / on-prem instances, and alerts when a deployment would exceed the licence count. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS License Manager — manages BYOL licences across AWS and on-prem fleets
AWS Marketplace — catalogue for buying third-party AMIs and SaaS subscriptions
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend trends and forecasts
AWS Resource Groups — groups arbitrary AWS resources by tag for batch operations
questions.explanation: License Manager helps track BYOL (Bring Your Own License) software deployments on EC2, prevents launching instances that would violate license terms, and provides a centralized dashboard for license inventory. The other options are incorrect: AWS Marketplace — catalogue for buying third-party AMIs and SaaS subscriptions; it does not manage BYOL licence counts, track on-prem installations, or enforce per-instance licence seat limits. AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend trends and forecasts; it does not track BYOL software licences, enforce per-seat license limits, or flag overuse across on-prem and cloud fleets. AWS Resource Groups — groups arbitrary AWS resources by tag for batch operations; it does not track software licence attaches to instances or enforce licence counts for BYOL products.

questions.q: An enterprise wants AWS to set up a multi-account 'landing zone' for them — pre-baked OUs, guardrails enforced via SCPs, a 'log archive' account, an 'audit' account, an Account Factory for new accounts. They want this in a few clicks, not via custom CloudFormation. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS Data Center Inventory
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements
AWS IAM role lifecycle manager
AWS Control Tower
questions.explanation: Control Tower builds a Landing Zone with: Log Archive account, Audit account, and an Account Factory. Guardrails (preventive = SCPs, detective = Config Rules) enforce compliance automatically across all accounts. The other options are incorrect: AWS Data Center Inventory — not a real AWS service; no AWS product provides pre-baked multi-account landing zone setup with automated OUs and audit accounts. AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements; it does not set up multi-account landing zones with SCP guardrails, log-archive accounts, or account factory provisioning. AWS IAM role lifecycle manager — not a real AWS service; no AWS product uses that name for managing multi-account landing zones or pre-baked audit account structures.

nodes.title: AWS analytics services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: AWS offers a suite of managed analytics services covering data warehousing, stream processing, interactive querying, and BI. The Cloud Practitioner exam tests which service to use for each scenario.

flashcards.front: Amazon Redshift — primary use case?
flashcards.back: Columnar data warehouse for petabyte-scale SQL analytics on structured data; not for OLTP or real-time streaming.

flashcards.front: Amazon Kinesis vs SQS — when to choose Kinesis?
flashcards.back: Kinesis for real-time ordered streaming with multiple consumers and replay; SQS for decoupled task queues with at-least-once delivery.

flashcards.front: Amazon Athena — how does it query data?
flashcards.back: Serverless interactive SQL on data stored in S3; no infrastructure to manage, pay per query (per TB scanned).

flashcards.front: AWS Glue role in an analytics pipeline?
flashcards.back: Managed ETL service: crawls data sources to build a Data Catalog, then runs serverless Spark jobs to transform and load data.

questions.q: An analytics team runs SQL queries over 500 TB of clickstream data. The workload is read-heavy, scans large columns of a few facts at a time, joins to dimension tables, and benefits from columnar compression + MPP (massively parallel processing). Which AWS service?
choices: ElastiCache — in-memory key-value cache for sub-millisecond data reads
RDS for MySQL/PostgreSQL — managed OLTP relational database optimised for transactional data
Amazon Redshift — managed columnar data warehouse with massively parallel processing
DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value and document store for fast single-key data access
questions.explanation: Redshift is AWS's managed data warehouse for analytics (OLAP). Uses columnar storage and MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) to run complex analytical queries across petabytes of data. The other options are incorrect: ElastiCache — in-memory key-value cache for sub-millisecond data reads; not a massively parallel SQL engine designed for scanning columnar analytics facts at petabyte scale. RDS for MySQL/PostgreSQL — managed OLTP relational database optimised for transactional data; not a massively parallel columnar processing engine for petabyte analytics. DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value and document store for fast single-key data access; not a massively parallel SQL data warehouse for complex analytics over petabytes.

questions.q: A telemetry pipeline must ingest 1 million events/sec from IoT devices, retain them ordered for 24-168 hours, and let multiple consumers replay the stream (Lambda, Firehose to S3, Analytics with windowing). Which AWS service is the streaming primitive?
choices: Amazon RDS — managed relational database for persistent transactional data
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — managed, shard-partitioned
Amazon S3 — durable object store that can act as a Kinesis Firehose destination
Amazon SQS — pull-based message queue with visibility timeout
questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is the streaming primitive: shard-partitioned, ordered within a shard, retention 24-168 hours, multiple consumers can replay. The other options are incorrect: Amazon RDS — managed relational database for persistent transactional data; it is not a real-time stream ingestion primitive for 1 million events per second. Amazon S3 — durable object store that can act as a Kinesis Firehose destination; it is not a real-time stream ingestion service capable of one-million-events-per-second ingest. Amazon SQS — pull-based message queue with visibility timeout; messages are consumed once and deleted by a single consumer group with no ordered replay capability for multiple independent consumers.

questions.q: A team wants to run ad-hoc SQL queries DIRECTLY against parquet/CSV/JSON files stored in S3, with NO database to provision, billed per TB scanned. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon RDS — managed relational database
Amazon Athena — serverless interactive SQL directly over parquet/CSV/JSON files
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) — moves databases between engines and to AWS
AWS Glue — managed ETL service whose Data Catalog integrates with Athena
questions.explanation: Athena is serverless ANSI SQL over data in S3 using Presto/Trino. Billed per TB scanned. Uses the Glue Data Catalog. DMS is a migration tool. The other options are incorrect: Amazon RDS — managed relational database; data must be loaded into the engine before SQL queries can run directly; it is not billed per-query-scanned for ad-hoc analysis. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) — moves databases between engines and to AWS; it does not run SQL queries directly against parquet/CSV/JSON files or bill per data scanned. AWS Glue — managed ETL service whose Data Catalog integrates with Athena; Glue itself runs ETL jobs and is billed per DPU-hour, not by the data directly scanned per query.

questions.q: A team wants a managed ETL service to (a) crawl source data, build a data catalog with schemas, (b) author and run Spark / Python jobs that transform S3 / RDS / Redshift data, (c) all serverless. Which AWS service?
choices: VPC Reachability Analyzer — a networking diagnostic tool
AWS CodePipeline — a managed CI/CD pipeline for software delivery
AWS Glue — serverless ETL with Crawlers + Data Catalog + Spark/Python jobs
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — a real-time streaming primitive for event ingest
questions.explanation: AWS Glue provides: Data Catalog (metadata repository for all your data sources), ETL jobs (serverless Spark-based transformations), and Crawlers (auto-discover schema from S3, RDS, etc.). The other options are incorrect: VPC Reachability Analyzer — a networking diagnostic tool; it is not a serverless ETL service and does not run Spark or Python jobs or build a data catalog. AWS CodePipeline — a managed CI/CD pipeline for software delivery; it does not provide serverless Spark/Python ETL jobs or a crawler-based data catalog. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — a real-time streaming primitive for event ingest; it is not a serverless batch ETL service and does not run Spark or Python crawling jobs.

questions.q: Finance asks BI for monthly KPI dashboards over Athena/Redshift/RDS data, accessible in a browser, no servers to operate, with per-reader pricing. Which AWS service fits?
choices: Amazon CloudWatch — operational-metrics dashboards over AWS infrastructure metrics
Amazon QuickSight — serverless BI service with dashboards over S3 / Redshift
AWS Glue — managed ETL service for cataloguing and transforming data
AWS CloudTrail — control-plane audit logs of AWS API calls
questions.explanation: QuickSight connects to dozens of data sources and enables self-service BI with SPICE (in-memory computation engine). ML Insights adds anomaly detection and forecasting. Pay-per-session pricing model. The other options are incorrect: Amazon CloudWatch — operational-metrics dashboards over AWS infrastructure metrics; not a BI tool over Athena, Redshift, or RDS data with per-reader pricing. AWS Glue — managed ETL service for cataloguing and transforming data; does not render BI dashboards over Athena, Redshift, or RDS for finance users. AWS CloudTrail — control-plane audit logs of AWS API calls; not a BI dashboard tool over Athena, Redshift, or RDS data with per-reader pricing.

nodes.title: AWS cost management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: AWS provides several tools to monitor, forecast, and reduce spending. The Cloud Practitioner exam asks which tool to use for billing analysis, budgets, and rightsizing recommendations.

flashcards.front: AWS Cost Explorer vs AWS Budgets?
flashcards.back: Cost Explorer: visualise and analyse past and forecasted spend. AWS Budgets: set spend/usage thresholds and receive alerts when approaching them.

flashcards.front: What does AWS Trusted Advisor's cost pillar check?
flashcards.back: Identifies idle or underutilised resources (e.g., low-CPU EC2, unattached EBS), Reserved Instance optimisation, and savings plan coverage gaps.

flashcards.front: Three ways to reduce AWS compute costs?
flashcards.back: Reserved Instances (1–3 yr commitment, up to 72% off), Savings Plans (flexible compute discount), and Spot Instances (spare capacity, up to 90% off).

flashcards.front: AWS Cost Allocation Tags — purpose?
flashcards.back: User-defined key-value pairs on resources; activate in Billing Console to break down costs by team, project, or environment in Cost Explorer.

questions.q: An architect needs to estimate the MONTHLY cost of a planned deployment (10 EC2 m6i.xlarge + 5 TB S3 Standard + 1 RDS db.m5.large + 100 GB data transfer) BEFORE provisioning anything. Which AWS tool produces a per-service estimate from the catalogue pricing?
choices: AWS Cost Explorer — analyses already-incurred monthly cost data by service and tag
AWS Pricing Calculator — public web tool for estimating monthly cost from catalogue list
AWS Budgets — alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold on a live deployment
AWS Trusted Advisor — provides best-practice recommendations on running infrastructure
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator lets you estimate monthly costs for AWS services before you deploy them. Cost Explorer analyzes existing costs; Budgets sets alerts. The other options are incorrect: AWS Cost Explorer — analyses already-incurred monthly cost data by service and tag; it is not a tool for estimating future transfer costs or pricing a proposed architecture before deployment. AWS Budgets — alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold on a live deployment; it is not a pre-deployment estimation tool and does not estimate the cost of anything before you deploy it. AWS Trusted Advisor — provides best-practice recommendations on running infrastructure; it does not estimate pricing or model catalogue costs before any deployment.

questions.q: A FinOps analyst wants to (a) chart historical spend per service / per tag / per linked account, (b) compare last quarter to this, (c) drill into cost spikes. The analysis is over ALREADY-INCURRED costs, not estimates. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS Pricing Calculator — a free pre-deployment estimation tool for a proposed architecture
AWS Budgets — sets cost and usage thresholds for an account and sends alerts on spikes
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises and analyses actual AWS cost
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for compliance reports
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer lets you analyze historical cost trends, identify cost drivers, forecast future spend, and find optimization opportunities with detailed filtering and charting. The other options are incorrect: AWS Pricing Calculator — a free pre-deployment estimation tool for a proposed architecture; it does not let you drill into historical service spend or compare actual versus forecast cost by period. AWS Budgets — sets cost and usage thresholds for an account and sends alerts on spikes; it does not chart historical service-level spend or provide the analytical views Cost Explorer offers. AWS Artifact — self-service portal for compliance reports; it has no cost visualisation, historical account spend analysis, or cost-spike detection capability.

questions.q: A finance team wants to be alerted when AWS spend hits 50%, 80%, and 100% of the monthly budget. The control must also support automatic actions (e.g., stop EC2 instances, apply an IAM policy) on threshold breach. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS Cost Explorer alerts only — provides historical and forecast charts
AWS Budgets — set monthly cost or usage budgets at 50/80/100% thresholds with email/SNS alerts
AWS Trusted Advisor budget module — surfaces cost-optimisation checks but does not directly emit
Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms only — fires on metrics like CPU
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets lets you define cost/usage/RI coverage budgets with SNS email/SMS alerts. Budget Actions can automatically apply IAM policies or stop EC2/RDS instances when thresholds are crossed. The other options are incorrect: AWS Cost Explorer alerts only — provides historical and forecast charts but cannot directly trigger budget-driven email or automated stop-EC2 actions at thresholds. AWS Trusted Advisor budget module — surfaces cost-optimisation checks but does not directly emit threshold alerts at 50/80/100% or apply policy actions. Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms only — fires on metrics like CPU; supports custom cost metrics but is not the canonical AWS service for monthly cost budgets and actions.

questions.q: An architect needs to forecast the monthly cost of a PROPOSED architecture (Lambda + DynamoDB + S3 + CloudFront + Route 53) BEFORE deploying anything. The tool must use AWS list prices and produce a per-service breakdown. Which AWS tool?
choices: AWS Bills — shows past monthly spend by account, service, and tag for charges already incurred
AWS Invoice Manager — handles invoicing for AWS Organizations payers
AWS Cost Saver Report — not a documented AWS product
AWS Pricing Calculator — free web tool that estimates monthly cost for proposed architectures
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator (calculator.aws.amazon.com) helps estimate costs upfront. Model EC2 instance types, storage, data transfer, and other services to build a cost estimate for budget approval or comparison. The other options are incorrect: AWS Bills — shows past monthly spend by account, service, and tag for charges already incurred; it is not a pre-deployment pricing tool for estimating a proposed architecture's future cost. AWS Invoice Manager — handles invoicing for AWS Organizations payers; it is not a tool for estimating future prices or modelling proposed deployment costs. AWS Cost Saver Report — not a documented AWS product; no canonical AWS tool uses that name for estimating deployment prices.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A workload runs the SAME m5.large fleet 24×7 with no changes for the next 3 years. The finance team wants the BIGGEST possible compute discount in exchange for a multi-year commitment. Which EC2 pricing model fits?
choices: On-Demand per-second pricing — pays the highest hourly rate and carries no commitment
Spot Instances — up to 90% off the On-Demand rate
Reserved Instances with a 3-year all-upfront term — up to 72% discount in exchange
Dedicated Hosts — physical-host isolation billing model used for licensing compliance
questions.explanation: For a STEADY, multi-year workload, the deepest discount comes from 3-year all-upfront Reserved Instances (up to 72%) or Compute Savings Plans (similar). On-Demand has NO commitment and NO discount. Spot is cheaper but interruptible. The other options are incorrect: On-Demand per-second pricing — pays the highest hourly rate and carries no commitment or discount in exchange for steady multi-year compute usage. Spot Instances — up to 90% off the On-Demand rate but interruptible; unsuitable for a steady multi-year workload that cannot tolerate reclaim events. Dedicated Hosts — physical-host isolation billing model used for licensing compliance; not the deepest-discount steady-multi-year-workload option for EC2 compute.

questions.q: A new AWS account holder is reading the Free Tier offer. AWS publishes three categories: ALWAYS-FREE services, 12-MONTH free usage for new accounts, and SHORT-TRIAL free for specific services. Which describes the Free Tier correctly?
choices: The Free Tier covers ALL services for the account lifetime with no limits
The Free Tier mixes 12-months-free offers for new accounts
The Free Tier covers only EC2 t-class instances for the first 30 days
The Free Tier is identical to a Reserved-Instance commitment with a specific short upfront payment
questions.explanation: AWS Free Tier includes: 12-month free (new accounts) — e.g., 750hr/month EC2 t2.micro; Always free — e.g., 1M Lambda requests/month; Trial — e.g., 2 months Amazon Redshift. The other options are incorrect: The Free Tier covers ALL services for the account lifetime with no limits — false; the Free Tier mixes 12-months-free offers for new accounts, always-free monthly allowances, and short-term trials. The Free Tier covers only EC2 t-class instances for the first 30 days — false; the Free Tier spans multiple services and mixes 12-months-free tiers, always-free allowances, and short-term trial offers. The Free Tier is identical to a Reserved-Instance commitment with a specific short upfront payment — false; Free Tier grants are always-free or time-limited with no payment commitment.

questions.q: A finance team compares EC2 cost models: (a) ~12 months of free usage on small instance types, (b) per-hour pay-as-you-go, (c) 1- or 3-year commitment with 40-72% discount, (d) interruptible spare capacity at up to 90% off. Which mapping is correct?
choices: All four EC2 cost models have the same effective hourly rate
Spot is dedicated long-running reserved capacity contracted for the full usage period
Reserved is more expensive than On-Demand at every comparable instance size
Free Tier = 12-mo free; On-Demand = pay-as-you-go; Reserved = 1/3-yr commit discount; Spot = interruptible spare capacity
questions.explanation: EC2 pricing: On-Demand (full price, flexible), RI Standard (fixed type, ~72% off, 1-3yr), RI Convertible (~66% off, can change type), Spot (bid on spare capacity, cheapest, interruptible with 2-min notice), Savings Plans (flexible commitment). The other options are incorrect: All four EC2 cost models have the same effective hourly rate — false; Free Tier provides free usage, On-Demand bills on-demand, Reserved gives discounts, and Spot uses interruptible spare capacity at steep reductions. Spot is dedicated long-running reserved capacity contracted for the full usage period — false; Spot provides interruptible spare-capacity instances priced hourly, not committed months-long terms. Reserved is more expensive than On-Demand at every comparable instance size — false; Reserved Instances provide a significant discount over On-Demand in exchange for a 1- or 3-year usage commitment.

questions.q: A platform team manages 40 AWS resources across 3 environments. They want to declare the entire stack as code in JSON or YAML files, version-control it, do change-set previews before applying, and roll back on failure. Which AWS service is the native infrastructure-as-code engine?
choices: Elastic Beanstalk — a PaaS that deploys application code and manages a stack of EC2, ELB, and Auto Scaling
OpsWorks — managed Chef and Puppet configuration management for an EC2 stack
AWS CloudFormation — declarative JSON/YAML templates over arbitrary AWS resources, with change sets
Systems Manager — fleet operations (patching, run-command, parameter store)
questions.explanation: AWS CloudFormation allows you to define AWS infrastructure as JSON or YAML templates and deploy it in a repeatable, automated way. The other options are incorrect: Elastic Beanstalk — a PaaS that deploys application code and manages a stack of EC2, ELB, and Auto Scaling; it does not manage arbitrary AWS resource stacks via declarative templates. OpsWorks — managed Chef and Puppet configuration management for an EC2 stack; it does not use JSON or YAML templates to declaratively define change sets across arbitrary AWS resource types. Systems Manager — fleet operations (patching, run-command, parameter store); it does not define or deploy a full declarative infrastructure stack from templates.

questions.q: A team needs a HIERARCHICAL key/value config + secret store for app config: dev/prod/region scoping via the path key, AT REST encryption via KMS for SecureString entries, version history per parameter, and a generous free tier. Which AWS service fits (without Secrets Manager's automatic rotation features)?
choices: AWS Secrets Manager — supports rotation and KMS encryption for secrets
S3 bucket storing config files — works for configuration but has no native KMS SecureString tier
EC2 fleet manager operations — manages instance patching and sessions
Systems Manager Parameter Store — hierarchical, KMS-encrypted SecureString, version history
questions.explanation: Parameter Store stores config data (DB strings, feature flags, AMI IDs) hierarchically (e.g., /prod/db/password). Free for standard parameters. SecureString type encrypts with KMS. Alternative to hardcoded config. The other options are incorrect: AWS Secrets Manager — supports rotation and KMS encryption for secrets; it is a paid service charged per secret rather than the free standard-tier hierarchical store suited for plain app configuration. S3 bucket storing config files — works for configuration but has no native KMS SecureString tier, hierarchical parameter path lookup, or built-in version history for individual keys. EC2 fleet manager operations — manages instance patching and sessions; it does not provide hierarchical parameter storage, SecureString tier, or version history for configuration values.

questions.q: An operations engineer wants to scale capacity based on demand for: (a) EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group, (b) DynamoDB read/write capacity, (c) ECS service desired-count, (d) Aurora read replicas. AWS offers a unified service that orchestrates scaling across all of these. Which?
choices: Auto Scaling is only available for EC2
AWS Compute Optimizer — recommends right-sizing of EC2, EBS, and Lambda based on usage history
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes incoming requests across registered targets
AWS Auto Scaling — orchestrates dynamic scaling across EC2 ASG, DynamoDB, ECS
questions.explanation: Auto Scaling policies: Target Tracking (e.g., CPU at 70%), Step Scaling (add 2 instances when CPU > 80%), Scheduled Scaling (predict load). Scaling out = add instances, Scaling in = remove instances. The other options are incorrect: Auto Scaling is only available for EC2 — false; AWS Auto Scaling orchestrates dynamic scaling across EC2 ASGs, DynamoDB tables, Aurora replicas, ECS services, and Lambda provisioned concurrency. AWS Compute Optimizer — recommends right-sizing of EC2, EBS, and Lambda based on usage history; it does not orchestrate live scaling or automatically adjust capacity in real time. Elastic Load Balancing — distributes incoming requests across registered targets; it does not orchestrate or auto-scale the backend capacity that handles those requests.

questions.q: A team needs a managed relational database with: (a) MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatibility (zero application change), (b) auto-scaling storage up to 128 TB, (c) up to 15 low-latency cross-AZ read replicas, (d) standard AWS billing per second. Which managed RDS engine fits ALL four?
choices: DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value store
ElastiCache for Redis — in-memory key-value cache with auto-scaling cluster nodes
Amazon Aurora — managed RDBMS with auto-scaling storage to 128 TB
Amazon Redshift — petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse with auto-scaling storage
questions.explanation: Aurora is AWS's cloud-native relational database. It auto-scales storage, replicates across 3 AZs with 6 copies, and offers serverless options. Fully managed within RDS. The other options are incorrect: DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value store; it is not MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatible and does not provide low-latency read replicas in a relational engine the way Aurora does. ElastiCache for Redis — in-memory key-value cache with auto-scaling cluster nodes; fast but not a durable relational database with auto-scaling storage and SQL latency guarantees. Amazon Redshift — petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse with auto-scaling storage; not MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatible and not designed for OLTP latency workloads.

questions.q: An RDS engineer compares two HA-vs-scaling options: (A) a synchronous standby in a different AZ that the engine auto-fails-over to on primary failure; (B) asynchronous COPY replicas in the same or other Region that take read traffic to scale OUT reads. Which mapping is correct?
choices: Multi-AZ and Read Replicas are functionally interchangeable
Read Replicas are for point-in-time backup
Multi-AZ = synchronous standby for HA; Read Replicas = asynchronous read scaling
Multi-AZ is for cross-Region DR
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ: synchronous standby in different AZ for failover HA — automatic failover ~1-2min. Read Replicas: asynchronous copies for read scaling — promotes manually for DR. Both can exist simultaneously. The other options are incorrect: Multi-AZ and Read Replicas are functionally interchangeable — false; Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby failover for high availability while Read Replicas provide asynchronous scaling for read throughput. Read Replicas are for point-in-time backup — false; automated backups handle that; Read Replicas use asynchronous replication for scaling read queries, not for synchronous failover standby. Multi-AZ is for cross-Region DR — false; Multi-AZ is an in-Region synchronous standby HA mechanism; cross-Region DR uses asynchronous Read Replicas in other Regions.
